name: Michael Branicky
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; earned B.S. from Case Western Reserve (1987) and M.S. (1990), then Sc.D. from MIT (1995). Major recognition (IEEE Fellow, 2016) and senior faculty roles came decades later.
early_history_summary: Branicky completed electrical engineering degrees at Case Western Reserve and a Sc.D. at MIT under Sanjoy Mitter, with early research fellow work at MIT CSAIL and a short NASA Ames stint. He later chaired EECS at CWRU and became a professor at the University of Kansas.
evidence_summary: Michael Branicky is an academic control-systems researcher whose documented career path runs through CWRU degrees (1987–1990), MIT Sc.D. (1995), faculty and chair roles at CWRU, and later a professorship at the University of Kansas. Birth year is not published; assuming a typical early-20s bachelor's implies age ~26 during mid-PhD years without an independently famous dated breakthrough. IEEE Fellowship arrived in 2016.

name: Anita Sarkeesian
milestone_by_age_26: No material breakthrough by age 26 found; she launched the Feminist Frequency blog/nonprofit around 2009 (age ~25–26) as a student project, but widespread recognition and material impact arrived with the May 2012 Kickstarter for Tropes vs. Women in Video Games (age ~28–29) and subsequent viral coverage.
early_history_summary: Born near Toronto to Iraqi Armenian immigrant parents, Sarkeesian moved to California as a teen, earned a B.A. from CSUN (2007) and M.A. from York University (2010). She started Feminist Frequency while still a graduate student; national fame followed the 2012 Kickstarter and harassment campaign.
family_context_summary: Born and raised near Toronto to Iraqi Armenian parents who emigrated to Canada in the 1970s; family later moved to California when she was a teenager.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having media/tech domain expertise.
evidence_summary: Anita Sarkeesian (b. 1983) built early feminist media criticism through Feminist Frequency starting ~2009, but the independently verifiable material milestone—Kickstarter funding and mass media attention for Tropes vs. Women—occurred in 2012 when she was about 28–29. Later awards (GDC Ambassador, TIME 100) and Feminist Frequency’s Peabody came well after age 26. The student-era blog launch is not treated as a material breakout under the eligibility bar.

name: Brendan Burns
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; completed a Ph.D. in robotics at UMass Amherst in 2007 after a B.A. from Williams, then worked in industry before co-creating Kubernetes at Google (announced 2014), well after typical mid-20s.
early_history_summary: Burns earned a B.A. in computer science and studio art at Williams College, then a Ph.D. in computer science (robotics) at UMass Amherst (2000–2007). He later joined Google, co-founded Kubernetes with colleagues, and moved to Microsoft as a corporate VP for Azure cloud-native platforms.
evidence_summary: Brendan Burns is best known for co-founding Kubernetes at Google (public 2014) and later leading Azure cloud-native work at Microsoft. Education timelines place his Ph.D. completion in 2007 after multi-year graduate study, implying age well over 26 by the Kubernetes launch. No independently dated material breakthrough by age 26 was found in reviewed sources.

name: Kim Mai Cutler
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; documented career is a multi-year journalism path (WSJ, Bloomberg, TechCrunch) followed by partnership at Initialized Capital. Birth year and any early breakout by 26 are not independently verified in reviewed sources.
early_history_summary: Grew up in Cupertino, California, and spent about a decade as a technology and finance journalist before joining Initialized Capital as a partner focusing on early-stage startups and housing/urban tech themes.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Cupertino, California (Apple’s hometown); additional family financial or domain details not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Kim-Mai Cutler is a Bay Area tech journalist-turned-VC (Initialized Capital) known for TechCrunch coverage of Silicon Valley housing and startups. No Wikipedia biography or independently dated age-26 milestone was found; public profiles emphasize a decade of reporting before venture work rather than a youthful breakout.

name: Anita Borg
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; self-taught programming job began ~1969 (age ~20) at a small insurance company, but Ph.D. (NYU, 1981), Systers (1987), Grace Hopper Celebration (1994), and the Institute for Women and Technology (1997) all came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born Anita Borg Naffz in Chicago (1949), she grew up in Illinois, Hawaii, and Washington. She taught herself to program while working at an insurance company, later earned a Ph.D. in computer science from NYU (1981), and built a research career at DEC and Xerox PARC while founding major women-in-computing institutions.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago; childhood also included Palatine, Illinois; Kaneohe, Hawaii; and Mukilteo, Washington. Family financial/domain details not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Anita Borg (1949–2003) became a defining advocate for women in computing via Systers, the Grace Hopper Celebration, and the institute later renamed AnitaB.org. Those institutional milestones occurred in her late 30s and 40s. By age 26 she had only begun self-taught programming work, not a dated public breakthrough.

name: Fred Brooks
milestone_by_age_26: Completed a Harvard Ph.D. in applied mathematics/computer science under Howard Aiken in 1956 at age 25, joined IBM, and by December 1957 (age 26) had co-invented and filed the patent on the Stretch program-interrupt system with Dura Sweeney—foundational work on IBM’s first transistorized supercomputer.
early_history_summary: Born in Durham, North Carolina, Brooks earned a physics B.S. from Duke (1953) and SM/Ph.D. at Harvard under Howard Aiken (1955–1956). Recruited into IBM’s Stretch project as a new graduate, he co-designed a generalized interrupt mechanism and later led System/360 and OS/360 before founding UNC’s computer science department.
family_context_summary: Born April 19, 1931, in Durham, North Carolina, and grew up in the Raleigh/Durham region; family socioeconomic details are sparsely documented beyond regional middle-class educational access.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as a computing or engineering family apprenticeship.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard under Aiken, IBM Stretch pipeline, Duke physics, interrupt patent, early computer architecture
evidence_summary: Fred Brooks moved rapidly from Duke physics into Harvard’s pioneering computing program under Howard Aiken, finishing a Ph.D. at 25 and joining IBM’s Stretch supercomputer project. By age 26 he had co-filed a foundational interrupt-system patent that became standard in modern computers. Later he managed System/360 and OS/360, coined “computer architecture,” founded UNC’s CS department, and wrote The Mythical Man-Month, earning the Turing Award (1999). Early advantage was elite institutional pipeline and mentor access rather than family-domain inheritance.
starting_point: Born in Durham, North Carolina, in 1931; raised in the Raleigh/Durham region and educated at Duke before Harvard.
current_position: Died November 17, 2022, at age 91 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina; final role: founding Kenan Professor of Computer Science at UNC (retired 2015), Turing Award laureate.

trajectory.event: Graduated with a B.S. in physics from Duke University.
Completed Ph.D. in applied mathematics/computer science at Harvard under Howard Aiken and joined IBM.
Co-invented and filed the Stretch program-interrupt system patent with Dura Sweeney while architecting IBM’s Stretch supercomputer.
Became project manager for IBM System/360 and OS/360 and founded the UNC Chapel Hill computer science department.
Left IBM after completing major System/360 leadership work; continued as UNC faculty.
Published The Mythical Man-Month, establishing Brooks’s law and shaping software engineering practice worldwide.
Received the ACM Turing Award for contributions to computer architecture, operating systems, and software engineering.
Died in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, after a long career as founding Kenan Professor at UNC.

name: Margaret Burnett
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; after studying math at Miami University (~1967–1970) she became an early woman software engineer/manager at Procter & Gamble, but her defining research (visual languages, end-user software engineering, gender HCI), Ph.D. (1987), and major awards (CHI Academy, ACM Fellow) came much later.
early_history_summary: Born 1949 in Springfield, Illinois; studied at Miami University of Ohio and later returned to academia for an M.S. (1981) and Ph.D. (1987) at the University of Kansas after industry and consulting work. She joined Michigan Tech faculty then Oregon State (1993), becoming a Distinguished Professor.
family_context_summary: Originally from Springfield, Illinois; further family financial or domain details not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Margaret Burnett is a leading HCI and end-user software engineering researcher at Oregon State. Early employment at Procter & Gamble around age 21 is notable for gender barriers of the era but is not a field-defining public milestone. Ph.D. and research leadership arrived in her late 30s and beyond.

name: Pei Cao
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; B.S. Tsinghua (1990), M.S. Princeton (1992), Ph.D. Princeton (1996 under Kai Li). Faculty at Wisconsin and industry roles (Tasmania Networks, Cisco, Google/YouTube) and PECASE (1998) came after the Ph.D.
early_history_summary: Cao trained in computer science at Tsinghua and Princeton, joined Wisconsin–Madison as assistant professor (1996–1999), founded Tasmania Network Systems (acquired by Cisco), then held technical leadership roles at Cisco and Google/YouTube focusing on web caching and search efficiency.
evidence_summary: Pei Cao is known for web caching and search infrastructure work spanning academia, a short-lived networking startup acquired by Cisco, and long tenure at Google/YouTube. Birth year is unpublished; degree years place Ph.D. completion around the late 20s and PECASE in 1998. No independently dated material milestone by age 26 was verified.

name: Linda Avey
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; B.A. biology from Augustana (1982, age ~22) and early research/sales roles in biopharma; co-founded 23andMe in March 2006 at age ~46.
early_history_summary: Born Linda Bahnson in South Dakota (1960), she earned a biology B.A. at Augustana University (1982), worked in academic research and biopharma sales/business development for decades (Affymetrix, Perlegen, Applied Biosystems, etc.), then co-founded 23andMe with Anne Wojcicki and Paul Cusenza in 2006.
family_context_summary: Born in South Dakota in 1960; family financial and occupational details not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Linda Avey co-founded consumer genetics company 23andMe in 2006 after roughly two decades in biopharma business development. That founding milestone was at age ~46; no independently verifiable material achievement by age 26 was found beyond ordinary early-career research/sales roles after college.

name: Anthony James Barr
milestone_by_age_26: Began designing the SAS statistical analysis system in 1966 at age 25–26 at North Carolina State, presenting core concepts in September 1966 (around his 26th birthday) after prior ANOVA and regression language work and IBM Federal Systems experience on the Formatted File System.
early_history_summary: Born in New York City (1940) and raised in Summit, New Jersey, Barr earned a B.S. in applied physics at NCSU (1962) and worked as a computing-center assistant, built early statistical programs, spent 1964–1966 at IBM Federal Systems on FFS at the Pentagon, then returned to create SAS’s language and data framework (1966–1968) before co-founding SAS Institute in 1976.
family_context_summary: Born in New York City and raised in Summit, New Jersey; inspired by inventor biographies and museum visits. Specific parental occupations and wealth not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as a computing/statistics family apprenticeship.
primary_early_advantage_tags: NCSU computing center, IBM FFS experience, statistical programming, SAS founding design, southern experiment stations network
evidence_summary: Anthony James Barr (b. 1940) built statistical programming systems as an NCSU graduate student, refined data-management skills at IBM Federal Systems, and by age 26 had begun the SAS language and architecture that became a global analytics platform. He later co-founded SAS Institute (largest early shareholder), sold his stake in 1979, and founded Barr Systems. Early leverage came from intensive domain practice and operational exposure rather than inherited capital or family industry position.
starting_point: Born in New York City in 1940 and raised in Summit, New Jersey; graduated Summit High School (1958) before NCSU applied physics.
current_position: Software entrepreneur and inventor associated with Barr Systems; co-creator of SAS who sold his SAS Institute stake in 1979; active in philanthropy and technical talks into the 2020s.

trajectory.event: Earned B.S. in applied physics (with honors) at NCSU and began computing-center statistical programming work.
Joined IBM Federal Systems Division at the Pentagon, rewriting components of the NIPS Formatted File System.
Began designing SAS and presented its conceptual ideas to southern agricultural statisticians in September 1966.
SAS 71, the first official version of SAS, was released for use by researchers.
Co-founded SAS Institute with Goodnight, Sall, and Helwig, holding the largest ownership stake (40%).
Sold his SAS Institute shares and later built Barr Systems around communications and remote-job-entry software.
With wife Olga, donated $1 million to the Cade Museum for Creativity and Invention for youth programming.

name: Brian Alvey
milestone_by_age_26: No material breakout milestone by age 26 found; by 1995–96 (age ~25–26) he had designed early TV Guide and BusinessWeek websites as a technical contractor, but the defining co-founding of Weblogs, Inc. (2003, age 33) and later AOL sale came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born March 6, 1970, in Falls Church, Virginia, and raised in Brooklyn. Built early commercial web properties in the mid-1990s, later co-founded Weblogs, Inc. with Jason Calacanis (sold to AOL ~2005), created Blogsmith, founded Crowd Fusion/Ceros, and later held CTO roles including WordPress VIP.
family_context_summary: Born in Falls Church, Virginia; grew up in Brooklyn. Family financial and occupational details not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Brian Alvey was an early commercial web designer/developer whose mid-1990s client work (TV Guide, BusinessWeek) shows competence before age 26 but not a independently famous company-building or product milestone. His material success narrative centers on Weblogs, Inc. (Engadget et al.) founded at age 33 and sold to AOL.

name: Kim Bruce

He spent 28 years as Frederick Latimer Wells Professor of Computer Science at Williams College before returning to Pomona as Reuben C. and Eleanor Winslow Professor, focusing on programming language design.
evidence_summary: Kim B. Bruce is a programming-languages academic known for long service building CS departments at Williams and Pomona. Birth year and any early dated breakthrough by age 26 are not established in reviewed sources; public recognition (e.g., ACM Distinguished Member, 2019) is late-career.
